slides.label: Intrinsic Constructions
slides.notes: Open the lecture by naming the chapter problem. Parallel transport was first pictured by watching arrows move on an embedded surface, but the intrinsic program asks for a rule that an inhabitant could run using only surface measurements. The deck will keep that test visible: every construction must use charts, metric lengths, tangent vectors, geodesics, or limiting comparisons rather than an ambient-space shortcut.

slides.label: Allowed Data
slides.notes: This slide separates geometric information from convenient scenery. The metric tells us lengths and angles in each tangent plane, geodesics tell us which small moves count as straight, and charts give labels for computation. The forbidden move is to decide transport by looking from outside the surface and projecting by eye. That projection can be useful as a verification bridge, but not as the intrinsic definition.

slides.label: Geodesic Ladder
slides.notes: Introduce the geodesic ladder as a finite construction that only asks for geodesic segments. Starting at a point with a tangent vector, step along the base curve, close a tiny geodesic quadrilateral, and read the transported vector from the next side. Emphasize that each rung is approximate, but shrinking the step size converts the ladder into a transport rule independent of the chosen drawing.

slides.label: Limit Comparison
slides.notes: The covariant derivative begins with a subtle subtraction problem: vectors based at different points do not live in the same vector space. The limit formula solves this by transporting the later vector back to the earlier tangent plane before subtracting. The local convergence figure helps students see why first-order comparisons stabilize even when the visible chord and arc measurements disagree at finite scale.

slides.label: Covariant Derivative
slides.notes: Now state the conceptual definition. A vector field along a curve has covariant derivative zero precisely when its successive values agree after intrinsic transport. If the derivative is nonzero, it measures the remaining tangent-plane change after the base-point motion has been accounted for. The diagram deliberately shows two tangent planes, because the operation is about comparing data after moving it into one common plane.

slides.label: Ordinary Versus Intrinsic
slides.notes: Use the ordinary derivative as the tempting but wrong first guess. Differentiating an embedded vector field in ambient space generally produces a component normal to the surface, which is not tangent data. Projecting back to the tangent plane gives the embedded formula for the Levi-Civita derivative, but the slide stresses that this is a check on the intrinsic rule, not the rule's source.

slides.label: Charts As Bookkeeping
slides.notes: Coordinates enter only after the intrinsic object is defined. In a chart, the correction terms Gamma record how the coordinate basis itself changes as the point moves. This lets students interpret the formula without treating Christoffel symbols as mysterious forces: they are bookkeeping coefficients that make the component derivative transform like a tangent vector rather than like a list of unrelated numbers.

slides.label: Loops Detect Curvature
slides.notes: Close the main arc by returning to loops. If an intrinsic transport rule carries a vector around a small loop and the vector returns rotated, the rotation is holonomy, and it previews curvature as a measured failure of transport to close. The point is operational: curvature is not first introduced as a tensor entry, but as the result of a repeatable experiment with arrows and small geodesic moves.

slides.label: Recap And Instructor Check
slides.notes: End with the three-step habit students should retain: transport first, compare in one tangent plane second, then pass to a limit. The instructor check asks students to diagnose which parts of a proposed construction are intrinsic and which smuggle in ambient information. That prepares the class for the next transport chapters, where holonomy and curvature turn this local derivative into global evidence.
